The BATTLE Trial: A Case Study on Biomarker-Guided, Bayesian Adaptive Trial

How a 255-patient lung-cancer trial made mandatory biopsies, a hierarchical probit model, and outcome-adaptive randomization work in practice — and what it still teaches us about designing modern biomarker-directed trials

1 Introduction

BATTLE-1 offers a rare practical example of adaptive trial design. It was the first completed prospective, biopsy-mandated, biomarker-based, adaptively randomized trial in previously treated non-small-cell lung cancer (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015). At MD Anderson Cancer Center, 255 heavily pretreated patients were assigned to four oral targeted therapies using a Bayesian model updated with fresh biopsy biomarkers and 8-week outcomes. (Kim et al. 2011; Zhou et al. 2008).

BATTLE is a valuable teaching case for three reasons. First, its design is thoroughly documented, including the statistical model, adaptive-randomization algorithm, futility rules, and operating-characteristic targets (Zhou et al. 2008; Liu and Lee 2015; Lee, Gu, and Liu 2010). Second, its operational lessons are as important as its statistics: a multidisciplinary team developed a pipeline to biopsy patients, classify eleven biomarkers, and assign treatment within about two weeks (Kim et al. 2011; Tam et al. 2013; Liu and Lee 2015). Third, its limitations are candidly reported, including issues with biomarker grouping, burn-in duration, fragmented eligibility, and population drift (Liu and Lee 2015; Kim et al. 2011).

2 Clinical and scientific context (circa 2005)

2.1 The therapeutic plateau BATTLE attacked

By 2005, treatment options for metastatic NSCLC after first-line chemotherapy offered only modest survival gains (Herbst, Heymach, and Lippman 2008). At the same time, dramatic responses to the EGFR inhibitor gefitinib were observed in selected subgroups, and activating EGFR mutations were identified as the underlying predictor of sensitivity (Lynch, Bell, and Sordella 2004). The BR.21 trial subsequently showed a modest survival benefit with erlotinib in unselected patients and linked benefit to EGFR mutation status and gene copy number (M.-S. Tsao, Sakurada, and Cutz 2005).

Although the FDA approved erlotinib for previously treated NSCLC in November 2004 without molecular selection (Cohen, Johnson, and Pazdur 2005), an EGFR companion diagnostic was not approved until May 2013 (2013). Thus, when BATTLE was conceived, targeted therapies and predictive biomarkers were available, but prospective biomarker-guided treatment assignment had not yet been implemented in NSCLC (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015).

2.2 Why a new trial architecture was needed

The trialists at MD Anderson — Edward S. Kim, Roy S. Herbst, Waun Ki Hong, Ignacio Wistuba, and the biostatistics team led by J. Jack Lee — faced a combinatorial problem that classical phase II designs handle poorly (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015):

  • Many agents, many markers. Four targeted agents (erlotinib, vandetanib, erlotinib + bexarotene, sorafenib) each plausibly worked only in marker-defined subgroups. The conventional alternative — 20 separate single-arm studies (4 agents × 5 marker classes) — would be slow, wasteful, and statistically fragile.
  • Unknowable markers in advance. Which biomarker truly predicted benefit was unknown before the trial; a design that locked in subgroup definitions at protocol time risked answering the wrong question.
  • Stale tissue. Biomarkers were usually assessed on archived diagnostic tissue, which may not reflect the biology of a tumor that had relapsed after multiple therapies (Liu and Lee 2015).

The BATTLE answer was architectural: one umbrella protocol, four parallel phase II sub-studies, a mandatory fresh biopsy for every patient, prespecified biomarker classes, and a Bayesian engine that reallocated future patients toward treatments performing well in their marker class as outcomes accumulated (Kim et al. 2011; Zhou et al. 2008).

2.3 Why the 8-week disease-control endpoint

Everything in an adaptive design lives or dies with how fast the outcome arrives. BATTLE chose disease control at 8 weeks (DCR@8w) — complete response, partial response, or stable disease by RECIST at week 8 — as the primary endpoint (Kim et al. 2011). The choice had empirical support: a Southwest Oncology Group analysis published while BATTLE was in development showed that disease control at 8 weeks predicted clinical benefit (survival) in advanced NSCLC (Lara, Redman, and Kelly 2008). It also had pragmatic virtues that a biostatistician should appreciate: it is quickly and objectively assessable, it suits the cytostatic profile of targeted agents (where tumor shrinkage is rare but stabilization is meaningful), and it turns around fast enough to inform randomization of the next patient (Kim et al. 2011; Zhou et al. 2008). The design paper was explicit that this short-turnaround property is what makes outcome-adaptive randomization viable at all (Zhou et al. 2008).

3 The BATTLE program at a glance

Fact box — what is documented about BATTLE-1

BATTLE-1 was a randomized phase II, single-center (MD Anderson Cancer Center), open-label umbrella trial with four parallel phase II sub-studies, activated on November 30, 2006 and completed accrual on October 28, 2009. It enrolled 341 patients, of whom 255 were randomized (equal randomization for the first 97, outcome-adaptive randomization for the remaining 158). The primary endpoint was 8-week disease control (DCR@8w). Approval came from the MD Anderson IRB and the U.S. Department of Defense; an independent Data and Safety Monitoring Board (chaired by Donald A. Berry) monitored the trial. Funding came in part from DoD grant W81XWH-6-1-0303 and NCI Cancer Center Support Grant CA016672, with support also acknowledged from Merck Research Laboratories and Bayer HealthCare (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015). Sub-study registrations on ClinicalTrials.gov: umbrella protocol NCT00409968, erlotinib NCT00410059, vandetanib (ZD6474) NCT00410189, erlotinib + bexarotene NCT00411632, sorafenib NCT00411671 (all activated November 2006).

Table 1 collects the headline facts and Figure 1 places them in time; Table 2 details what each arm tested and where each drug stood regulatorily when the trial ran.

            "Primary paper\n(Cancer Discov,\nJun 2011)",
            "BATTLE-2 opens\n(Jun 2011)",
            "BATTLE-2 FDA meeting;\nIDE waiver (Jan 2013)",

  grp = c("Program", "Program", "Program", "Program",
          "Follow-on", "Follow-on (regulatory)", "Follow-on")
)
timeline_plot(events, xbreaks = seq(2005, 2017, 2))

Two registry facts complete the picture. First, patients who progressed could re-enter the trial with a new biopsy and be re-randomized — hence the 17 second and 1 third randomizations documented in the CONSORT diagram (Kim et al. 2011). Second, a front-line companion program, BATTLE-FL (NCT01263782), was later registered and completed with 64 participants, but this article focuses on BATTLE-1 and BATTLE-2, which carry the published methods lessons (Liu and Lee 2015).

Why the umbrella-plus-sub-studies structure mattered

Structurally, BATTLE-1 was “one protocol, four trials”: a single consent, a single screening biopsy, and a single randomization engine serving four parallel phase II sub-studies (Liu and Lee 2015). For a biostatistician the important consequence is shared learning: every patient’s outcome updated one common model, so information flowed across sub-studies through the hierarchical prior — something four separately conducted single-arm trials cannot do. The trialists explicitly credited this “all patients under one roof” feature with improving patient comparability and efficiency relative to sequential single-arm studies (Liu and Lee 2015).

4 Inside the design: objectives, biomarker engine, and the Bayesian machinery

4.1 What the trial promised to deliver

BATTLE aimed both to evaluate targeted therapies and establish a platform for estimating treatment-specific disease control rates (DCRs) within biomarker groups. Under one protocol, posterior probabilities governed three decisions (Zhou et al. 2008; Liu and Lee 2015):

  1. Success: Declare an arm × marker-group cell successful if
    \(\Pr(\gamma_{jk} > 0.30 \mid \text{data}) \ge 0.80\) (Equation 8), relative to the historical 30% DCR (Kim et al. 2011; Lara, Redman, and Kelly 2008).
  2. Futility: After adaptive randomization began, suspend a cell if
    \(\Pr(\gamma_{jk} > 0.50 \mid \text{data}) \le 0.10\) (Equation 7). Suspension was reversible (Zhou et al. 2008; Liu and Lee 2015).
  3. Adaptive randomization: Assign patients among eligible, active treatments in proportion to the posterior mean DCR for their marker group (Equation 5) (Zhou et al. 2008).

Simulation calibrated these thresholds to limit the success rate to 20% under a 30% true DCR, while achieving at least 80% power at a 60% DCR and up to 95% at an 80% DCR (Zhou et al. 2008; Liu and Lee 2015). The deliberately liberal 20% type I error reflected the platform’s exploratory purpose: prioritizing potentially effective treatments for confirmation rather than prematurely discarding them (Kim et al. 2011; Zhou et al. 2008).

Figure 2 shows the flow. Two design choices deserve attention. First, the burn-in stage had a specific statistical job: equal randomization built the “prior probability of disease control for a given treatment in a given marker group” that the adaptive engine would consume afterwards (Kim et al. 2011). The plan called for at least 80 equally randomized patients, sufficient — the designers judged — for every marker-group cell to contain at least one completed treatment (Kim et al. 2011); in the event, equal randomization covered 97 patients (~38% of randomized patients), a point the team later flagged as a lesson (Section 6.2) (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015). Second, eligibility restricted the adaptive engine: arms had treatment-specific eligibility criteria, and only 14% of enrolled patients were eligible for all four arms, so the randomization denominator Ω shrank patient by patient (Liu and Lee 2015).

4.3 From 11 biomarkers to 5 marker groups

The biomarker panel was fixed in 2005 and prespecified before activation (Kim et al. 2011). Tumors were tested for mutations of EGFR, KRAS, and BRAF; copy number (FISH) of EGFR and the cyclin D1 gene (CCND1); and protein expression (IHC) of VEGF, VEGFR-2, RXRα, RXRβ, RXRγ, and cyclin D1 — eleven markers in total (Kim et al. 2011). Because dichotomizing eleven markers yields \(2^{11} = 2{,}048\) possible profiles, the team collapsed them into five ranked marker groups, assigning each patient to the highest-ranked positive group (ranked by the strength of available 2005-era evidence), with a fifth group for patients negative for everything or with missing/incomplete data (Liu and Lee 2015; Kim et al. 2011):

Keep Table 3 in mind — the grouping itself became the trial’s most-cited self-criticism (Sections 7 and 8): strong single-marker effects (e.g., EGFR mutation for erlotinib) were diluted when bundled with weaker markers in the same class (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015).

4.4 The Bayesian hierarchical probit model

BATTLE’s outcome model is a hierarchical probit model — elegant, easy to Gibbs-sample, and pedagogically ideal because every piece has a trial-level meaning (Zhou et al. 2008). For patient \(i\) in arm \(j \in \{1,2,3,4\}\) and marker group \(k \in \{1,\dots,5\}\), define \(y_{ijk} \in \{0,1\}\) as the 8-week disease-control indicator. Introduce a latent variable \(z_{ijk}\):

\[ y_{ijk} = \mathbf{1}\{z_{ijk} > 0\}, \qquad z_{ijk} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{jk},\, 1) \tag{1}\]

Here \(\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}\) is the indicator function, \(z_{ijk}\) is an unobserved “tolerance” that tips the patient into disease control when positive, and the variance is fixed at 1 for identifiability (the probit scale has no free scale parameter) (Zhou et al. 2008). The disease-control probability for the cell \((j,k)\) is then a smooth function of the cell mean \(\mu_{jk}\):

\[ \gamma_{jk} \;=\; \Pr(y_{ijk} = 1) \;=\; \Pr(z_{ijk} > 0) \;=\; \Phi(\mu_{jk}), \tag{2}\]

where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. Intuition: \(\mu_{jk}\) is just the probit transform of the cell’s DCR — e.g., a DCR of 0.46 corresponds to \(\mu \approx 0.10\), and 0.58 to \(\mu \approx 0.20\).

The hierarchy enters through the prior on the cell means. Within an arm, the five marker-group means are exchangeable around an arm-level effect \(\phi_j\); the arm effects are themselves exchangeable around zero (Zhou et al. 2008):

\[ \mu_{jk} \sim \mathcal{N}(\phi_j,\, \sigma^2) \quad (k = 1,\dots,5), \qquad \phi_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, \tau^2) \quad (j = 1,\dots,4) \tag{3}\]

with \(\sigma^2 = \tau^2 = 10^6\) as the default vague configuration (Zhou et al. 2008). Read Equation 3 as two dials of partial pooling: small \(\sigma^2\) makes the marker groups within an arm share information heavily (each group’s estimate is pulled toward the arm effect \(\phi_j\)); small \(\tau^2\) makes the arms share information with each other. BATTLE ran these dials essentially open (vague priors), so borrowing happened only where the data themselves were concordant — the model “learns how much to borrow” from the observed pattern of subgroup results (Zhou et al. 2008; S. M. Berry et al. 2010).

Given the observed disease-control indicators, the posterior combines a probit likelihood with the normal priors:

\[ p(\mu, \phi \mid \text{data}) \;\propto\; \prod_{j=1}^{4} \prod_{k=1}^{5} \prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}} \Phi(\mu_{jk})^{y_{ijk}} \left[1 - \Phi(\mu_{jk})\right]^{1 - y_{ijk}} \;\times\; \prod_{j,k} \mathcal{N}(\mu_{jk} \mid \phi_j, \sigma^2) \;\times\; \prod_{j} \mathcal{N}(\phi_j \mid 0, \tau^2) \tag{4}\]

The symbols in Equation 4: \(n_{jk}\) is the number of patients randomized to arm \(j\) within marker group \(k\); \(\mu\) collects all twenty cell means and \(\phi\) the four arm effects. The trial team computed these posteriors by Gibbs sampling from the full conditionals — a workload that was heavy for 2006 but is trivial today, and that BATTLE-1 automated in R behind a web service (Section 6) (Zhou et al. 2008; Liu and Lee 2015).

Interpretation — why a probit rather than a logit?

The probit link is not a substantive claim about biology; it is a computational convenience. With normal priors on \(\mu_{jk}\), the full conditionals are (truncated) normals, so Gibbs sampling is exact and fast — no Metropolis–Hastings tuning in the middle of a live trial. A logistic model with the same hierarchy (used later for BATTLE-2, (Lee, Gu, and Liu 2010)) would deliver nearly identical inferences; the choice reflects 2006-era Bayesian computation practice, an excellent example of letting the computing environment shape — not distort — the statistics.

Figure 3 makes the “borrowing strength” idea concrete with a small simulation.

Show the R code 
set.seed(7)
k_grp <- 8; n_per <- 8; kappa <- 10
mu_sim   <- rnorm(k_grp, qnorm(0.40), 0.35)
p_true   <- pnorm(mu_sim)
x_sim    <- rbinom(k_grp, n_per, p_true)
p_raw    <- x_sim / n_per
p_bar    <- sum(x_sim) / (k_grp * n_per)
p_shrunk <- (x_sim + kappa * p_bar) / (n_per + kappa)
shr <- data.frame(group = factor(1:k_grp), p_raw, p_shrunk)
ggplot(shr, aes(x = group, xend = group)) +
  geom_segment(aes(y = p_raw, yend = p_shrunk), colour = "grey60",
               linewidth = 0.6, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(aes(y = p_raw), shape = 21, size = 2.6, fill = "white", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(aes(y = p_shrunk), size = 2.6, colour = pal[1]) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Simulated marker-group cell (one arm)",
       y = "8-week DCR estimate",
       title = "Partial pooling: raw vs. shrunk subgroup estimates") +
  annotate("text", x = 7.6, y = 0.92, size = 2.9,
           label = "open = raw subgroup rate\nfilled = shrunk toward arm mean")

4.5 The adaptive-randomization engine

Once every one of the 20 cells (4 arms × 5 groups) contained at least one patient with a known outcome, randomization switched from equal to outcome-adaptive. For the next patient in marker group \(k\), the probability of assignment to arm \(j\) was proportional to the posterior mean disease-control rate of that cell, with two safeguards (Zhou et al. 2008):

\[ w_{jk} \;=\; \frac{\hat\gamma_{jk}}{\sum_{\omega \in \Omega}\hat\gamma_{\omega k}}, \qquad \hat\gamma_{jk} = \max\!\big\{\, \mathbb{E}[\gamma_{jk} \mid \text{data}],\; 0.10 \,\big\} \tag{5}\]

In Equation 5, \(\hat\gamma_{jk}\) is the posterior mean DCR for arm \(j\) in group \(k\) (floored at 0.10 so no non-suspended arm ever becomes essentially unreachable — the trial’s explicit minimum-allocation device (Zhou et al. 2008)), and \(\Omega\) is the set of arms that are both non-suspended for futility and eligible for that patient (recall: only 14% of patients were eligible for all four arms (Liu and Lee 2015)). The published worked example (Zhou et al. 2008) makes the weights tangible: if the current posterior mean DCRs in a marker group were 0.6, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1, the assignment probabilities become 0.50, 0.25, 0.17, and 0.08.

Two remarks for the practicing statistician. First, this is covariate-adjusted adaptive randomization: the weights are computed within marker group, so the adaptation respects the stratification — the trial learns “which arm works best for tumors like this one” rather than a single global winner. Second, BATTLE-1’s rule is the plainest member of the broader family of Bayesian adaptive-randomization rules popularized by Thall and Wathen, who add a power smoothing so that early, noisy estimates do not over-steer allocation (Thall and Wathen 2007):

\[ w_j^{(m)} \;=\; \frac{\bar p_j^{\,q(m)}}{\sum_{\ell} \bar p_\ell^{\,q(m)}}, \qquad q(m) \;=\; \frac{m/4 + 8}{m}, \tag{6}\]

where \(m\) indexes trial progress, \(\bar p_j\) is the current probability that arm \(j\) is (or performs) best, and \(q(m) > 1\) early (dampening) falls below 1 later (sharpening). BATTLE-1 used the unsmoothed proportional form of Equation 5; its successor BATTLE-2 instead bounded the randomization probabilities (0.2–0.8 in stage 1, 0.1–0.9 in stage 2) to prevent extreme allocations from either noise or premature certainty (Liu and Lee 2015). If you implement one of these designs today, the choice among {no smoothing, power smoothing, probability bounds} is exactly the kind of decision to justify by simulation. Figure 4 shows what the BATTLE-1-style engine does in silico when seeded with the trial’s own marginal response rates.

Show the R code 
set.seed(41)
truth_ar <- c(E = 0.34, V = 0.33, EB = 0.50, S = 0.58)
n_pat <- 244
s_ar <- n_ar <- rep(0, 4)
w_hist <- matrix(NA_real_, n_pat, 4)
for (i in seq_len(n_pat)) {
  phat   <- (s_ar + 1) / (n_ar + 2)      # Beta(1,1) posterior mean
  w_arms <- pmax(phat, 0.10)             # 10% floor
  w_arms <- w_arms / sum(w_arms)
  w_hist[i, ] <- w_arms
  j <- sample(4, 1, prob = w_arms)
  n_ar[j] <- n_ar[j] + 1
  s_ar[j] <- s_ar[j] + rbinom(1, 1, truth_ar[j])
}
colnames(w_hist) <- names(truth_ar)
w_df <- as.data.frame(w_hist) |>
  mutate(patient = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(-patient, names_to = "arm", values_to = "probability")
w_df$arm <- factor(w_df$arm, levels = names(truth_ar),
                   labels = c("erlotinib", "vandetanib",
                              "erlotinib + bexarotene", "sorafenib"))
ggplot(w_df, aes(patient, probability, colour = arm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.25, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Patient arrival (order)", y = "Assignment probability",
       title = "Simulated adaptive weights under BATTLE-like marginal DCRs") +
  annotate("text", x = 15, y = 0.265, size = 2.9, colour = "grey40",
           label = "equal randomization (0.25)")

4.6 Futility monitoring: suspension, not execution

After adaptive randomization began, each new outcome re-triggered a futility check for every cell. A cell was suspended — patients in marker group \(k\) could no longer be randomized to arm \(j\) — whenever

\[ \Pr\{\gamma_{jk} > 0.50 \mid \text{data}\} \;\le\; 0.10, \tag{7}\]

i.e., when the data made it unlikely (posterior probability ≤ 10%) that the cell’s true DCR exceeded the 50% target (Zhou et al. 2008; Liu and Lee 2015). Three features of this rule reward attention. It is cell-specific: the same arm could stay open for one marker group while suspended for another — the entire point of a biomarker-guided design. It is reversible: if later data (e.g., from other marker groups borrowed through the hierarchy) lifted the posterior back above the boundary, the cell reopened (Zhou et al. 2008). And there is no early stopping for efficacy: success was only declared at trial end, so adaptation and inference could never race each other (Zhou et al. 2008). The success rule itself, applied to every cell at the trial’s close, was

\[ \Pr\{\gamma_{jk} > 0.30 \mid \text{data}\} \;\ge\; 0.80, \tag{8}\]

i.e., a posterior probability of at least 0.80 that the cell’s true DCR exceeds the 30% historical benchmark (Zhou et al. 2008; Kim et al. 2011).

Show the R code 
m_seq <- 1:80
fut_curve <- function(p_true) {
  sapply(m_seq, function(mm) 1 - pbeta(0.50, mm * p_true + 1, mm * (1 - p_true) + 1))
}
fut_df <- data.frame(
  m = rep(m_seq, 2),
  prob = c(fut_curve(0.30), fut_curve(0.55)),
  scenario = rep(c("true DCR 30% (futile)", "true DCR 55% (active)"), each = length(m_seq)))
ggplot(fut_df, aes(m, prob, colour = scenario)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.10, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[1], pal[3])) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number()) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.003, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Evaluable patients in the cell (arm × marker group)",
       y = "Pr(DCR > 0.50 | data)  [log scale]",
       title = "Cell-level futility statistic vs. the 0.10 suspension boundary") +
  annotate("text", x = 45, y = 0.115, size = 2.9, colour = "grey35",
           label = "suspension boundary (0.10)")

5 The biomarker engine: real-time tissue from relapsed lung cancer

5.1 The pipeline, step by step

The boldest requirement of BATTLE was not statistical. Every enrolled patient had to consent to a fresh tumor biopsy after relapse — in a population already heavily treated, with lesions that are often hard to reach (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015). Figure 6 reconstructs the documented pipeline.

Show the R code 
bx <- data.frame(
  x = c(4.6, 4.6, 4.6, 4.6, 4.6),
  y = c(9.2, 7.35, 5.5, 3.65, 1.7),
  w = c(7.2, 6.6, 7.2, 8.2, 7.2),
  h = c(1.25, 1.0, 1.15, 1.55, 1.15),
  fill = c("#D9E8F5", "#DFF2E4", "#FDEBD0", "#E8E0F0", "#FBE3E0"),
  size = c(2.8, 2.75, 2.75, 2.6, 2.8),
  label = c(
    "Image-guided core-needle biopsy\n(1–3 fresh cores, ≥ 2 required)",
    "Formalin fixation immediately,\nin the interventional radiology suite",
    "Molecular pathologist H&E review within 24 h\n(adequate = ≥ 200 malignant cells)",
    "11-biomarker panel: mutations (EGFR, KRAS, BRAF);\nFISH (EGFR, CCND1); IHC (VEGF, VEGFR-2, RXRα/β/γ, cyclin D1)",
    "Marker group assigned →\nadaptive randomization engine"))
ba <- data.frame(x = c(4.6, 4.6, 4.6, 4.6), xend = c(4.6, 4.6, 4.6, 4.6),
                 y = c(8.58, 6.73, 4.88, 2.83), yend = c(8.38, 6.53, 4.68, 2.63))
flow_diagram(bx, ba, ylim = c(0.6, 10)) +
  annotate("text", x = 9.15, y = c(9.2, 7.35, 5.5, 3.65, 1.7), size = 2.6,
           colour = "grey35", hjust = 0.5,
           label = c("day 0", "day 0", "≤ day 1", "≤ 2 weeks", "≤ 2 weeks")) +
  labs(title = "From needle to randomization in about two weeks")

The pipeline had a second, forward-looking layer: alongside the clinical-trial cores, additional tissue (and blood/serum) was banked for discovery — the raw material for later BATTLE-derived papers on KRAS variant biology, an EMT resistance signature, and sorafenib sensitivity signatures (Section 7.4) (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015).

6 Implementation and operations: where adaptive designs actually live


## The information system
BATTLE treated the adaptive design as a real-time information system. An integrated web application tracked patients from registration and biopsy through biomarker classification, randomization, 8-week assessment, and follow-up. Data were stored in MD Anderson’s CORe environment and a study-specific SQL Server database (Liu and Lee 2015). R code, invoked through web services, automatically updated posterior DCRs, randomization probabilities, and futility decisions whenever an outcome was recorded (Liu and Lee 2015). This infrastructure illustrates the practical costs of adaptive trials: timely data entry, quality control, computation, and specialized software (Lee and Chu 2012).
Endpoint timeliness was critical. Automated reminders prompted coordinators to schedule week-8 scans and escalated outcomes overdue by more than two weeks (Liu and Lee 2015). A multidisciplinary endpoint committee, blinded to treatment assignment, adjudicated RECIST outcomes before they entered the randomization algorithm (Liu and Lee 2015).
::: {.callout-tip appearance=“simple”} ## Why blinded adjudication mattered Each 8-week outcome influenced allocations for future patients. Knowledge of treatment could bias assessments, particularly stable-disease classifications, and propagate that bias through the adaptive algorithm. Blinded adjudication is therefore an important safeguard in outcome-adaptive trials (Liu and Lee 2015). :::
## Implementation lessons
BATTLE required close coordination among clinicians, radiologists, pathologists, pharmacists, nurses, programmers, coordinators, and statisticians (Liu and Lee 2015). Its retrospective evaluation identified five main lessons (Liu and Lee 2015; Kim et al. 2011):

  1. Marker grouping diluted signals. Combining EGFR mutations with copy-number changes weakened predictive performance, while several prespecified markers were uninformative. Marker groupings should remain flexible when prior evidence is limited.
  2. Burn-in delayed adaptation. Requiring observations in every cell postponed adaptive randomization until approximately 40% of patients had enrolled. The investigators later recommended adapting after about 20–25%.
  3. Eligibility restricted adaptation. Only 14% of patients were eligible for all four treatments, so most allocations occurred within restricted arm sets \(\Omega\) (Equation 5).
  4. Population drift changed eligibility. Increasing proportions of smokers and patients previously treated with erlotinib altered the available treatment sets. Adaptive trials should monitor such drift and consider covariate adjustment.
  5. Adaptation depends on biological separation. Outcome-adaptive randomization offers limited gains when treatments or biomarkers do not meaningfully discriminate outcomes (Liu and Lee 2015; Lee, Chen, and Yin 2012).
    ::: {.callout-note appearance=“simple”} ## BATTLE-2: redesigning around the lessons BATTLE-2 introduced adaptive randomization from the first patient, bounded allocation probabilities, and no prespecified marker groups. Candidate biomarkers were screened before the trial and evaluated through a Bayesian two-stage Lasso strategy. The design also added a stage-1 Go/No-Go decision, futility monitoring from patient 71, and a target of 400 evaluable patients, with at least 80% power and a 10% type I error rate. Following a January 2013 FDA meeting, the trial received an investigational device exemption waiver (Liu and Lee 2015; Lee, Gu, and Liu 2010; Gu, Yin, and Lee 2013; Gu et al. 2016). :::

7 Documented results: what 244 evaluable patients showed

7.1 Patient flow and exposure

Figure 7 lays out the documented flow. One quarter of enrolled patients (86 of 341) never reached randomization — the price of a biopsy-mandated design in a rapidly declining population — and the arm-level counts already hint at the adaptation to come.

The randomized population was characteristically hard: median age 62 (range 26–84), 54% male, 63% adenocarcinoma, 69% former smokers, ECOG 0–1 in 85%, median two prior chemotherapy regimens, 45% previously treated with erlotinib, and 33% with prior brain metastases. Mutation prevalence: EGFR 15%, KRAS 20% (Kim et al. 2011).

7.2 Overall efficacy, and the primary endpoint

Among the 244 patients evaluable at 8 weeks, the overall DCR@8w was 46% (112/244), with no complete responses and only 9 partial responses — typical cytostatic activity for targeted agents in this setting. Median PFS was 1.9 months (95% CI 1.8–2.4), median OS 8.8 months (95% CI 6.4–10.6), and 1-year survival 35%. In a pre-specified-style landmark analysis anchored at week 8, patients with disease control lived longer (median 9.6 months, 95% CI 7.4–12.5) than those without (7.5 months, 95% CI 4.2–9.2; P = 0.018) (Kim et al. 2011). Treatment-related grade 3–4 toxicity was 6.5% and compliance exceeded 95% in every arm; sorafenib caused the most toxicity (treatment discontinuation in 19%, dose reductions in 21%) (Kim et al. 2011).

To visualize the marginal results with honest uncertainty, we recompute Wilson score intervals (Equation 9) from the documented counts and plot them in Figure 8 — a reconstruction of published summaries, not new inference on patient-level data:

\[ \tilde p = \frac{\hat p + z^2/(2n)}{1 + z^2/n}, \qquad \text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\gamma) = \tilde p \pm \frac{z}{1 + z^2/n}\, \sqrt{\frac{\hat p (1 - \hat p)}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4 n^2}} \tag{9}\]

In Equation 9, \(\hat p = x/n\) is the observed DCR in a cell with \(x\) disease-control successes among \(n\) evaluable patients and \(z = 1.96\) for a 95% interval; \(\tilde p\) is the interval’s center, pulled slightly toward 1/2 relative to \(\hat p\). The Wilson interval behaves well for the small cell counts (\(n\) as low as 3) that adaptive trials inevitably produce — unlike the Wald interval, it never leaves \([0,1]\) and stays sane near the boundaries.

Show the R code 
wilson <- function(x, n, z = 1.959964) {
  p <- x / n
  d <- 1 + z^2 / n
  ctr <- (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / d
  hw  <- (z / d) * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2))
  c(ctr - hw, ctr + hw)
}
arms_df <- data.frame(
  arm = c("Erlotinib", "Vandetanib", "Erlotinib +\nbexarotene", "Sorafenib"),
  x = c(20, 17, 18, 57),
  n = c(58, 52, 36, 98))
ci_ar <- t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(arms_df)), function(i) wilson(arms_df$x[i], arms_df$n[i])))
arms_df$pct <- 100 * arms_df$x / arms_df$n
arms_df$lo  <- 100 * ci_ar[, 1]
arms_df$hi  <- 100 * ci_ar[, 2]
ggplot(arms_df, aes(arm, pct, fill = arm)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.62, colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.09, linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 30, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(x, "/", n, "  (", round(pct), "%)")),
            vjust = -1.0, size = 3.0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal[1:4]) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 85), labels = percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "8-week disease control rate",
       title = "Marginal DCR@8w by arm (documented counts, Wilson 95% CIs)") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.62, y = 31.5, size = 2.9, colour = "grey35",
           hjust = 0, label = "historical 30% DCR benchmark")

Read Table 4 — visualized as a heatmap in Figure 9 — the way the design intended: down columns are conventional marginal results; across rows is the trial’s real hypothesis test — within a marker group, which targeted agent controls disease? Sorafenib’s 79% (11/14) in KRAS/BRAF-mutant tumors against 14% for erlotinib and 0% for vandetanib is the pattern a biomarker-guided trial exists to find, and it confirmed the prespecified hypothesis for sorafenib in that class (Kim et al. 2011).

7.4 Did adaptation actually happen? Yes — visibly

Equal randomization would have put ~64 patients per arm; Figure 10 plots the divergence. The documented final allocation — 105 to sorafenib versus 58 erlotinib, 52 vandetanib, 36 erlotinib + bexarotene — is the adaptive engine made visible: as evidence accumulated, the marginal DCR leader received increasingly more patients (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015).

7.5 The individual-marker story the grouping obscured

The team’s prespecified and exploratory single-marker analyses — run after the marker-group model had done its allocation work — sharpen the picture (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015):

  • EGFR mutation predicted better 8-week control on erlotinib (P = 0.04): 71% DCR in EGFR-mutant versus 29% in wild-type tumors (Liu and Lee 2015).
  • High VEGFR-2 expression predicted benefit from vandetanib (P = 0.05), consistent with the arm’s mechanism (Kim et al. 2011).
  • High cyclin D1 expression (P = 0.01) and EGFR amplification (P = 0.006) predicted benefit from erlotinib + bexarotene — the RXR/cyclin D1 hypothesis finally visible only at the individual-marker level (Kim et al. 2011).
  • For sorafenib, DCR was 64% in EGFR-wild-type tumors versus 33% for all other treatments combined (P < 0.001), with a trend in KRAS-mutant tumors (61% vs 32%, P = 0.11) (Kim et al. 2011); EGFR mutation (P = 0.01) and high polysomy (P = 0.05) predicted worse control on sorafenib (Kim et al. 2011).

Figure 11 draws these contrasts side by side.

               "KRAS-mutant: sorafenib vs\nall other arms"),
  lo = c(29, 22, 33, 32),
  hi = c(71, 61, 64, 61),
  p  = c("P = 0.04", "P not reported", "P < 0.001", "P = 0.11"))

7.6 Arm postscripts published after the main paper

Three of the four arms received dedicated final publications that deepen the results in instructive ways. The sorafenib analysis confirmed the marginal DCR of 58.2% (98 evaluable), median PFS 2.83 months (95% CI 2.04–3.58) and OS 8.48 months (95% CI 5.78–10.97); DCR was higher in EGFR-wild-type than EGFR-mutant tumors (P = 0.012), and a gene-expression “sorafenib sensitivity signature” built from cell lines and BATTLE biopsies separated PFS (3.61 vs 1.84 months, P = 0.026) (Blumenschein et al. 2013). The vandetanib report showed overall activity (DCR 33%, median PFS 1.81 months, median OS 6.5 months) with an exploratory hint of benefit from dual VEGFR/EGFR blockade in EGFR-mutant, TKI-resistant tumors but no overall survival advantage (A. S. Tsao et al. 2013). An elderly-subgroup analysis found signals such as better PFS with vandetanib in men aged 65–70 and with sorafenib in men over 70 (A. S. Tsao, Liu, and Lee 2012). Banked specimens additionally yielded the KRAS-variant biology analysis (Ihle, Byers, and Kim 2012) and the 76-gene EMT resistance signature (Byers, Diao, and Wang 2013).

Show the R code 
tt <- seq(0, 24, by = 0.05)
surv_df <- data.frame(
  t = rep(tt, 2),
  S = c(0.5^(tt / 1.9), 0.5^(tt / 8.8)),
  curve = rep(c("PFS (median 1.9 months)", "OS (median 8.8 months)"),
              each = length(tt)))
ggplot(surv_df, aes(t, 100 * S, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 8, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = 3, colour = "grey60") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[1], pal[4])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomization", y = "Event-free proportion",
       title = "Illustrative exponential reconstruction of the published medians") +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = 93, size = 2.9, colour = "grey35",
           label = "week 8: the primary endpoint's clock")

\[ S(t) = 0.5^{\,t / m} \tag{10}\]

In Equation 10, \(S(t)\) is the event-free proportion at time \(t\) and \(m\) the median event time in months; the exponential is the unique survival model in which the hazard is constant, and it is used here purely as a visual calibration device, not as an inferential claim.

8 Regulatory interactions, guidance, and the path to acceptance

Because adaptive and biomarker-guided designs live or die by regulatory acceptance, this section addresses the question directly and in two layers: what is documented about BATTLE’s own regulatory interactions, and how the surrounding regulatory framework evolved around trials like it. Where we move from record to interpretation, we say so.

8.1 What is actually documented about BATTLE and regulators

Fact box — documented regulatory touchpoints of the BATTLE program
  • Oversight of BATTLE-1 was conventional and documented: approval by the MD Anderson IRB and the U.S. Department of Defense, monitoring by an independent DSMB (chaired by Donald A. Berry), and standard IND-era handling of the investigational agents (Kim et al. 2011).
  • Agent status mattered. Two of the four agents were FDA-approved at the time (erlotinib, Nov 2004 (Cohen, Johnson, and Pazdur 2005); sorafenib, Dec 2005, for renal-cell carcinoma (Kane, Farrell, and Sabharwal 2006)); vandetanib was not approved anywhere until April 2011 (2011); the erlotinib + bexarotene combination was investigational (Kim et al. 2011). BATTLE-1 was thus an investigator-initiated phase II platform, not a registration program.
  • The documented FDA interaction belongs to BATTLE-2: “Due to its exploratory nature, BATTLE-2 has received the investigational device exemption (IDE) waiver after a meeting with the FDA in January 2013” (Liu and Lee 2015). The trial’s biopsy-and-biomarker workflow is what brings it into IDE territory, and the sponsor sought and documented FDA input on the adaptive design before opening stage 1 (trial registration NCT01248247; opened June 2011 at MD Anderson and Yale).
  • Industry engaged publicly: the primary BATTLE-1 paper drew a companion commentary from scientists at Merck Research Laboratories framing the trial as “a bold step toward improving the efficiency of biomarker-based drug development” and highlighting simultaneous therapeutics–diagnostics development (Rubin, Anderson, and Gause 2011); Merck scientists (D. Mauro, E. Rubin) later co-authored the BATTLE-2 primary paper (Papadimitrakopoulou et al. 2016).
  • To our knowledge, no public record documents a special FDA review of BATTLE-1’s adaptive features of the kind later formalized in FDA’s adaptive-design guidance processes — consistent with its role as an exploratory, single-center, non-registration platform. (This is a statement about the absence of public documentation, not about private interactions.)

8.2 Interpretation: what BATTLE did and did not change for regulators

Interpretation (clearly not a documented causal claim)

BATTLE was never a registration trial, and it left no documented regulatory decision trail of its own. Its regulatory significance is better understood as feasibility testimony and methodological exemplar: it demonstrated to sponsors and reviewers alike that biopsy-mandated, biomarker-stratified, adaptively randomized platforms can be executed and monitored, and its statistical grammar — hierarchical models, posterior decision thresholds, simulated operating characteristics, prespecified adaptation rules — is precisely the grammar the 2019 FDA guidance later asks sponsors to speak (2019a; Liu and Lee 2015; Lee and Chu 2012). Three specific contrasts between BATTLE-style exploration and registration expectations are worth teaching:

  1. Error budgets. A deliberate 20% per-cell type I error rate is defensible for discovery platforms; regulators evaluating confirmatory claims ask for controlled family-wise (or at least clearly bounded) error across the adaptation and subgroup structure — the EMA paper and FDA final guidance both make this central (2007, 2019a).
  2. Endpoint. An 8-week DCR enabled the adaptation but would not, by itself, support a therapeutic claim; registration examples of biomarker-guided approval (e.g., the erlotinib–cobas EGFR co-approval) rested on survival-benefit endpoints with validated diagnostics (2013; Cohen, Johnson, and Pazdur 2005).
  3. Device–drug coupling. BATTLE used biomarkers for allocation learning, not for device-regulated patient selection claims; the regulatory machinery for the latter (co-development, CDx PMA) is what later made biomarker-guided labels routine (2014, 2019b).

In our reading, BATTLE’s most durable regulatory contribution is cultural: along with I-SPY 2 (Barker et al. 2009), it normalized the idea that a trial’s decision engine can learn while protecting patients — and the eventual ICH E20 draft is, in effect, the codification of lessons from this generation of platform trials (2025; D. A. Berry 2012).

9 Legacy: BATTLE-2 and the platform-trial era

9.1 BATTLE-2: the redesign, honestly reported

BATTLE-2 (NCT01248247) redesigned the platform around every lesson of BATTLE-1: adaptive randomization from the first patient, stratified by KRAS status with probabilities bounded at 0.2–0.8 (stage 1) and 0.1–0.9 (stage 2); no prespecified marker grouping (>100 candidate markers screened pre-trial, refined in-trial via training–testing–validation and a Bayesian two-step Lasso); a Go/No-Go gate after stage 1; futility monitoring from patient 71; 450 planned enrollments (400 evaluable); and a documented FDA meeting (January 2013) with IDE waiver (Liu and Lee 2015; Lee, Gu, and Liu 2010; Gu et al. 2016; Gu, Yin, and Lee 2013). The design and other feature of the trial will be discussed in other article.

9.2 The era BATTLE helped open

Contemporaneous commentaries recognized the moment — “a new BATTLE in the evolving war on cancer” (Sequist, Muzikansky, and Engelman 2011), and, from Merck, “a bold step toward improving the efficiency of biomarker-based drug development” (Rubin, Anderson, and Gause 2011). The direct descendants are familiar. I-SPY 2 embedded biomarker-adaptive randomization with Bayesian “graduation” rules in breast cancer (Barker et al. 2009). NCI-MATCH and Lung-MAP made molecular screening plus biomarker-matched assignment national infrastructure (2024b, 2024a). Reviewers of adaptive oncology cite BATTLE as the completed proof-of-concept for Bayesian adaptive, biomarker-guided randomization (D. A. Berry 2012; Lee and Chu 2012; Liu and Lee 2015). And the specific design ideas — hierarchical borrowing across subgroups, posterior-probability decision rules, allocation floors and bounds, burn-in stages — are now standard vocabulary in trial-design software and ICH E20 discussions (2025; S. M. Berry et al. 2010).

10 Ten lessons for designing and analyzing biomarker-guided adaptive trials

  1. Operations are the design. The binding constraint on BATTLE was never computation; it was biopsy adequacy (82.9%), assay turnaround (2 weeks), and endpoint timeliness. Before promising any adaptation, measure — and prespecify minimum acceptable values for — the operational chain that feeds it (Tam et al. 2013; Liu and Lee 2015).
  2. Pick an endpoint that outruns accrual. Adaptive randomization only helps if outcomes arrive faster than patients. The 8-week DCR was chosen for exactly this property and had survival-prediction evidence behind it (Lara, Redman, and Kelly 2008; Zhou et al. 2008).
  3. Budget the burn-in, don’t let it happen to you. Equal randomization builds the prior, but a “wait until every cell is filled” rule handed the calendar to the sparsest subgroup (~40% of the trial ran equally). A fixed proportion (20–25%) or model-based readiness criteria are safer (Liu and Lee 2015).
  4. Don’t bundle biomarkers you mean to learn about. Grouping preserved degrees of freedom but diluted EGFR-mutation signal and wasted the trial’s sparsest groups on uninformative RXR markers. Group only when prior evidence is genuinely symmetric across constituents; otherwise model individual markers (Kim et al. 2011; Liu and Lee 2015).
  5. Keep allocation floors/bounds — and justify them by simulation. The 10% floor kept every open arm learnable; BATTLE-2’s 0.2–0.8 and 0.1–0.9 bounds prevent both starvation and premature commitment. Show that operating characteristics survive perturbing these constants (?@fig-sensitivity) (Zhou et al. 2008; Liu and Lee 2015).
  6. Simulate the eligibility structure, not just the biology. Only 14% of patients were eligible for all four arms; the effective randomization space is the intersection of futility, eligibility, and marker group. Your simulations should mimic that intersection (Liu and Lee 2015).
  7. State decision thresholds and their error trade-off in advance. Null 30% / target 50% / success at 80% posterior / futility at 10% posterior — all prespecified, all calibrated by simulation, with the 20% type I error rate defended openly as a screening choice (Zhou et al. 2008; Kim et al. 2011).
  8. Make futility reversible and adjudicate endpoints blinded. Cell-level suspension that can reopen, plus an endpoint review committee blinded to assignment, protects the integrity of the feedback loop into randomization (Zhou et al. 2008; Liu and Lee 2015).
  9. Watch for drift and say what adaptation does to comparisons. Monitor enrollment mix prospectively (BATTLE’s smokers/prior-erlotinib drift); plan covariate adjustment for between-arm contrasts, because adaptive allocation entangles arm with calendar time (Liu and Lee 2015).
  10. Separate the engine from the verdict. BATTLE’s adaptive machinery learned which cells were promising; it did not — and was never designed to — establish comparative efficacy. Design the confirmation path (randomized comparison, validated diagnostic, appropriate error budget) as part of the platform, not afterthought (Kim et al. 2011; 2007, 2019a).
